title: How he got on with Bill Boyd and Blackie Simmons; the band's teasing
summary: He sat in on radio and dance jobs with Bill Boyd's Cowboy Ramblers and then filled in for Blackie's pianist. The country musicians liked his blues playing and enjoyed teasing him for his naivete.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Can you tell me the circumstance of how you joined this first band, Blackie Simmons?

Well, I had been playing a few radio programs and dance jobs with Bill Boyd's Cowboy Ramblers. And he had already made arrangements to hire the pianist from Blackie Simmons, but liked my work better. I've forgotten Sonny somebody. He's that first one who made the first records with Bill Boyd. But he'd already made a commitment. And so whenever Blackie's pianist worked with him, I went over to take his place just automatically there. It was catch as catch can in those days, and as it is now, and sometimes it's awfully hard, even in big cities, much less small ones, to get fill-ins. You find that even in your audience, I guess. Is that true? Yeah.
Then you'd been playing with Bill Boyd before you joined Blackie Simmons.
Radio programs and just a few odd jobs scattered around.
Was Bill Boyd the first band you'd played with?
How did this come about? I mean, he was well known.

Yes, I went up there one day and started, went in there, and I don't know how. Somebody told me I played a little piano, and some friend carried me in and introduced me, gave me a build-up, and had me sit in with her for a few numbers, and they liked the way I played and laughed, and I was so little. Even when I graduated from school, I was about old, not old. I don't know how tall, but very, very short enough to get by as being 12 years old. Country, country, country. Grice and hay all over me.
How about the rest of the guys in the band?

Well, they were always good, too. They thought we looked kind of as, you know, kind of a kid or mascot or something in life, but they liked my playing very much, especially the blues. They liked that because that's been my heritage, you see. When we played the blues, I was on home ground.
Well, now, you said that you were a country at that time. How about the rest of the fellows, were they?

Yes, they were a country, too, but they'd been out in, they were from, when we say country, now let's qualify this. It has good aspects as well as unfavorable connotations. But my school, I'd come from a very sheltered background, and some of these musicians I worked with were from Crossford Railroad tracks, and they enjoyed just that much more of my naivety.

Yeah, always. You can imagine what it would be like. Brother, in those days, when you say you put a ball in that surrounding, man, that was really it. That would be too hard. Tate would have to be made in asbestos to take some of those things that would happen.
